abstract: This paper examines the prevalence and consumption of 'fake news'—false stories circulated largely through social media—in the context of the 2016 US presidential election. The authors discuss the economics underlying fake news and present new empirical data on how often such stories were seen and believed by American voters. They combine web browsing data, fact-checking archives, and an original online survey to estimate the reach and potential influence of fake news.
key_claims: Fake news circulated widely, particularly through social media, in the period before the 2016 election.
Social media was an important but not the dominant source of election news for Americans.
The scale and believability of fake news can be characterized empirically rather than through speculation alone.
Understanding fake news requires an economic framework analyzing the incentives to produce and share it.
methods: Analysis of web browsing data to measure news consumption patterns.
Use of archives from fact-checking websites to catalog fake news stories.
A new online survey to measure exposure to and belief in specific news stories.
Economic analysis of the market for fake news.
findings: About 14 percent of Americans called social media their most important source of election news.
Social media was an important but not dominant source of election news overall.
The paper quantifies consumption of fake news prior to the election (additional specific findings truncated in the available abstract).
contributions: Provides new empirical data on the consumption of fake news before the 2016 election.
Offers an economic framework for understanding the production and spread of fake news.
Integrates multiple data sources (browsing data, fact-checking archives, survey) to assess fake news reach and impact.
framing: The paper is positioned within the economics of media and information, applying economic reasoning to the emerging phenomenon of fake news and its role in democratic elections and public opinion formation.
